newsitem.title: BELGIUM: CARS CHEAPEST IN NETHERLANDS AND PORTUGAL.
newsitem.headline: CARS CHEAPEST IN NETHERLANDS AND PORTUGAL.

text.p: The Netherlands and Portugal are the cheapest places in the European Union to buy a car and Germany and France the most expensive, the European Commission said on Friday.
Commission data up until November 1, 1996 showed that 23 of the EU's 75 best-selling models were cheapest in the Netherlands while 21 were cheapest in Portugal.
Germany and France had the highest list prices of the 12 countries surveyed, each with 30 of the dearest models, followed by Britain with 15.

"Price differences exceeded 20 percent for 40 of the 75 models examined. This was particularly true for the Fiat Group, Ford , Opel , Citroen , Volkswagen , Nissan and Mitsubishi ," the Commission said in a statement.

It said German Fiat Punto list prices were 26.3 percentage points higher than in Portugal while British Ford Fiestas and Opel Astra/Kadetts were 26.8 and 32.8 percentage points respectively more expensive than their equivalents in Portugal.

"The difference between the lowest and the highest price for these models has increased in comparison to the previous survey. This is partly attributable to exchange-rate-induced price increases in the United Kingdom," the report said.
The Commission publishes six-monthly tables of car price differences in an attempt to push pricing trends towards a genuine single market for new vehicles.
Of the EU's 15 member countries Denmark, Finland and Greece are excluded from the survey on the grounds of the high taxes they levy on new vehicle sales, the Commission said.
Commission figures are all free of tax, meaning that EU bargain seekers should check their likely tax liabilities on a car before rushing to cheaper countries for new vehicles.
The EU executive urged any customers facing difficulties buying cheaper cars across EU borders, so-called parallel trading, to complain to its competition watchdogs.
The Commission said parallel trade in cars was being blocked in Germany, Belgium, Spain and the Netherlands.
"It was found that final customers still encounter obstacles in certain member states," it said.
In a related development, the European Commission has raided offices of German carmaker Mercedes-Benz AG and General Motors' Opel, an EU source told reporters on Friday.
Raids on Mercedes related to sales in all four named countries while those on Opel related only to Dutch sales.

The raids, in connection with alleged irregularities in vehicle pricing and distribution arrangements, were on similar grounds to current Commission investigations into Volkswagen and its subsidiary Audi, the source said.
